answer:
MAIN COMPUTATION COMPLETE (approved method: unweighted per-wave, per-cohort medians, listwise deletion, negatives and top-coded values retained).

(1) 3×3 MEDIAN FAMILY NET WEALTH TABLE (median $, n per cell):

| Wave | Black (1) | Hispanic (2) | Non-Black Non-Hispanic (3) | All races |
|------|-----------|--------------|----------------------------|-----------|
| 1985 | 1,600 (n=1,699) | 500 (n=2,631) | 3,500 (n=5,774) | 2,000 (n=10,104) |
| 1990 | 4,800 (n=1,528)  | 1,600 (n=2,431) | 12,972 (n=5,336) | 6,200 (n=9,295) |
| 1996 | 9,800 (n=1,368)  | 2,563 (n=2,114) | 42,600 (n=3,557) | 16,500 (n=7,039) |

Gap magnitude (code 3 vs others): vs Black: +1,900 (2.2×) in 1985 → +8,172 (2.7×) in 1990 → +32,800 (4.4×) in 1996. vs Hispanic: +3,000 (7.0×) → +11,372 (8.1×) → +40,038 (16.6×).

(2) ALL-RACE CONTEXT: overall wave medians 2,000 (1985), 6,200 (1990), 16,500 (1996); the non-Black non-Hispanic median exceeds the all-race median in every wave, while the Black and Hispanic medians sit below it in every wave.

(3) HYPOTHESIS (final answer):

"Hypothesis: From 1985 onward, the median family net wealth of non-Black, non-Hispanic respondents — the only available proxy for 'white' individuals in this dataset (1979 racial/ethnic cohort code 3) — is consistently and substantially higher than that of Black and Hispanic respondents, and the gap widens over time. In 1985, median family net wealth was $3,500 for non-Black non-Hispanic respondents (n=5,774), versus $1,600 for Black respondents (n=1,699) and $500 for Hispanic respondents (n=2,631) — about 2.2 times the Black median and 7 times the Hispanic median. By 1990 the gap had widened to $12,972 (n=5,336) versus $4,800 (n=1,528) and $1,600 (n=2,431) — about 2.7× and 8.1×. By 1996 it reached $42,600 (n=3,557), roughly 4.4× the Black median of $9,800 (n=1,368) and about 16.6× the Hispanic median of $2,563 (n=2,114). Four caveats bound this claim: (a) 'white' is operationalized as the 1979 non-Black non-Hispanic cohort, which also includes other non-Hispanic, non-Black groups, and race is recorded only once, in 1979; (b) wealth is family/household net wealth, not individual wealth; (c) figures are in nominal dollars and no deflator is available in the file, so part of the widening gap reflects inflation; (d) medians are unweighted and computed on shrinking, differentially attrited samples — retention of the 1979 cohort with observed wealth was 76.9%→71.1%→47.4% for the non-Black non-Hispanic group, 84.9%→76.3%→68.3% for Black, and 82.9%→76.6%→66.6% for Hispanic respondents across 1985→1990→1996 — so later-wave gaps may be biased in either direction and cannot be corrected without weights."

Limitations of the computation itself: top-coded tail values (per-wave caps; up to 2.0% of the 1996 sample) were retained but sit far above the medians and cannot alter them; negative net-debt values (e.g., 302 of 3,557 in 1996 for code 3) were retained as legitimate; no statistical tests of median differences were requested or performed.

payload.workflow: Loaded data/nls_raw.csv (12,686 rows × 61 cols). Verified exact column names, 0 duplicate IDs, race column with values {1,2,3} only, and fully numeric wealth columns. For each wave (1985, 1990, 1996) and each 1979 racial/ethnic cohort code, computed the unweighted median of family net wealth among respondents with non-missing wealth at that wave (listwise deletion), retaining negative net-debt values and per-wave top-coded tail values; reported n per cell, n_negative, n_at_cap, and retention vs the 1979 baseline, plus all-race wave medians for context. Executed script: analysis/median_wealth_by_race.py; output table: analysis/median_wealth_by_race_results.csv.
